reference.source: GeneReviews / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: SPG3A, caused by heterozygous ATL1 variants encoding atlastin-1, is the second commonest autosomal dominant HSP after SPG4 and the most frequent early childhood-onset dominant form
It usually presents as a pure HSP with symptom onset in the first years of life, sometimes mistaken for spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
The course is often relatively non-progressive or only slowly progressive, which is a helpful distinguishing feature from SPG4
Lower-limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantars predominate, with weakness usually mild
Occasional families show complicating features such as peripheral neuropathy or distal wasting
A dominant family history is common, but de novo variants occur and penetrance can vary
Treatment is symptomatic, focusing on antispasticity measures, gait, and physiotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary spastic paraplegias result from length-dependent, distal-predominant degeneration of the longest corticospinal axons. ATL1 encodes atlastin-1, a GTPase that mediates homotypic fusion of endoplasmic reticulum tubules and helps shape the tubular ER network, working in concert with other HSP proteins such as spastin and the REEP proteins. Variants impair ER morphogenesis and axonal transport within long motor neurones, and because the distal segments of these very long axons are most dependent on efficient membrane trafficking, they degenerate preferentially, producing the lower-limb-predominant spasticity.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary spastic paraplegias (e.g. SPG4, SPG31)
Metabolic disorders presenting with childhood spasticity
Structural spinal cord lesion or tethered cord
additionalInvestigations: Brain and spine MRI to exclude structural, perinatal, or white-matter causes
Genetic testing for ATL1 within an HSP panel, including dosage analysis
Trial of levodopa where dopa-responsive dystonia is a consideration
Nerve conduction studies if distal wasting or neuropathy is suspected
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics in young children
redFlags: Clear clinical progression or regression suggesting an alternative progressive disorder
Asymmetry, focal deficit, or a sensory level indicating a structural spinal lesion
Prominent bulbar or upper-limb involvement inconsistent with pure HSP
Diurnal fluctuation of symptoms suggesting a treatable dopa-responsive condition
reference.prognosis: SPG3A often runs a comparatively benign, slowly progressive or near-static course, and most affected individuals remain ambulant, frequently with better long-term mobility than later-onset dominant forms.
pitfalls: Labelling an early-onset case as cerebral palsy and missing a genetic, inheritable diagnosis
Assuming absence of family history excludes SPG3A given de novo variants
Failing to trial levodopa when the differential includes dopa-responsive dystonia
Overtreating spasticity to the detriment of functional support and gait
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine titrated to lower-limb tone, with botulinum toxin for focal muscle overactivity
Regular physiotherapy and stretching to prevent contractures, with ankle-foot orthoses to optimise the spastic gait from early childhood
Occupational therapy and educational support given the early-childhood onset that can mimic spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
Surveillance for contractures, gait change and foot deformity with orthopaedic review
Bladder assessment and antimuscarinic therapy if urinary symptoms develop
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, noting de novo variants and variable penetrance
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, physiotherapy and rehabilitation input
